h: A few things most visitors miss
p: Salisbury Cathedral was built remarkably quickly by medieval standards. The main body went up in around 38 years from 1220, which is why it has such a unified, all-of-a-piece look compared with cathedrals that were patched together over centuries. The spire came a little later, and it is worth stepping back on the lawn to take in just how slender it is.

Inside, keep your eyes peeled for the medieval clock in the nave. It is often described as one of the oldest working clocks in the world, and it has no face at all, because it was built to strike the hours rather than show them. Kids are usually fascinated by the chunky iron workings.

Magna Carta lives in the Chapter House, an octagonal room with a central column fanning out to the roof and a carved frieze of Old Testament scenes running round the walls. Give yourself a few minutes in there; the document is small and the lighting low to protect it, so let your eyes adjust.
Make sure you see the font too, a modern piece with a flowing water surface that reflects the windows above, and a favourite with photographers.

Allow around two hours for the cathedral and Close at a relaxed pace. Inside the Close, Mompesson House, a National Trust townhouse, and The Salisbury Museum are both easy add-ons. Then wander into the city centre, where the Market Place has hosted markets for centuries, and on a fine day follow the river path out to the water meadows for the classic view Constable painted.
